paragraphs: Hera said, “Sleep, why do you get such notions into your head? Do you think Zeus will be as eager to help the Trojans as he was for his own son? Come, I will give you one of the youngest of the Graces in marriage, and she will be yours—Pasithea, the one you have always wanted to marry.”

Sleep was glad to hear it. “Then swear it to me,” he answered, “by the dread waters of the river Styx. Put one hand on the bounteous earth and the other on the sheen of the sea, so that all the gods who live below with Cronus will be our witnesses, and will see that you truly give me one of the youngest of the Graces—Pasithea, whom I have always wanted to marry.”

Hera did as he asked. She swore the oath and called on all the gods of the nether world, the ones called Titans, as witnesses. When the oath was complete, the two wrapped themselves in a thick mist and hurried on, leaving Lemnos and Imbrus behind them. Soon they came to many-fountained Ida, mother of wild beasts, and to Lectum, where they left the sea and went on over land. The tops of the forest trees rustled beneath their feet. Sleep stopped here. Before Zeus could catch sight of him, he climbed a lofty pine—the tallest that lifted its head toward heaven on all Ida. He hid among the branches and sat there looking like the sweet-singing bird of the mountains, which the gods call Chalcis and men call Cymindis. Hera then went on to Gargarus, the topmost peak of Ida, and Zeus, driver of the clouds, saw her. The moment he did, he was filled with the same passionate desire for her that he had felt when they first enjoyed each other’s embraces and slept together without their dear parents knowing anything about it. He went up to her and said, “Why have you come here from Olympus, and with no chariot or horses to carry you?”

Then Hera told him a lie. “I am on my way to the end of the world,” she said, “to visit Oceanus, from whom all we gods come, and mother Tethys. They took me into their house, looked after me and raised me. I must go and see them to make peace between them. They have been quarreling, and are so angry that they have not slept together for a long time. The horses that will carry me over land and sea are waiting on the lowest slopes of many-fountained Ida, and I came here from Olympus specially to consult you. I was afraid you might be angry with me later if I went to the house of Oceanus without telling you.”

And Zeus said, “Hera, you can visit Oceanus some other time. For now let us give ourselves to love and to enjoying each other. Never has passion overpowered me like this, for goddess or mortal woman, as it does at this moment for you—not even when I loved the wife of Ixion, who bore me Pirithous, the peer of gods in counsel, nor Danae, the daintily-ankled daughter of Acrisius, who bore me the famed hero Perseus. Then there was the daughter of Phoenix, who bore me Minos and Rhadamanthus. There was Semele, and Alcmena in Thebes, by whom I fathered my lion-hearted son Heracles, while Semele became the mother of Dionysus, comforter of mankind. There was queen Demeter too, and lovely Leto, and yourself. But with none of these was I ever so much in love as I am now with you.”

Hera again answered him with a lie. “Most dread son of Cronus,” she exclaimed, “what are you saying? Would you have us make love here on the top of Mount Ida, where everything can be seen? What if one of the ever-living gods saw us sleeping together and told the others? It would be such a scandal that after I rose from your embrace I could never show myself in your house again. But if you are willing, there is a room your son Hephaestus made for me, and he gave it good strong doors. If that is what you want, let us go there and lie down.”

And Zeus answered, “Hera, you need not fear that god or man will see you. I will wrap both of us in a golden cloud so dense that not even the sun, for all his bright piercing beams, can see through it.”

With this the son of Cronus took his wife in his arms. At once the earth sprouted a cushion of fresh grass for them, with dew-bespangled lotus, crocus and hyacinth, so soft and thick that it lifted them well above the ground. They lay down there, and a fair cloud of gold covered them overhead, from which glittering dewdrops fell.

So the father of all things lay peacefully on the crest of Ida, overcome by sleep and love, with his wife in his arms. Meanwhile Sleep ran off to the ships of the Achaeans to tell earth-encircling Poseidon, lord of the earthquake. Having found him, he said, “Now, Poseidon, you can help the Danaans wholeheartedly and give them victory, though only for a short while, since Zeus is still sleeping. I have sent him into a sweet slumber, and Hera has beguiled him into going to bed with her.”

Sleep then left and went on his way among mankind, leaving Poseidon more eager than ever to help the Danaans. He darted out among the foremost ranks and shouted, “Argives, are we going to let Hector son of Priam take our ships and cover himself in glory? That is what he says he will do, because Achilles is still sulking at his ship. We will manage very well without him if we keep each other’s spirits up and stand by one another. So now, all of you, do as I say. Each of us should take the best and largest shield he can lay hands on, put on his helmet, and march out with his longest spear in his hand. I will lead you, and Hector son of Priam, rage as he may, will not dare to hold out against us. If any good, steady soldier has only a small shield, let him hand it to a worse man and take a larger one for himself.”

So he spoke, and they did as he said. The son of Tydeus, Odysseus and Agamemnon, wounded though they were, put the others in order and went everywhere arranging the exchanges of armor. The most valiant took the best armor and gave the worse to the worse man. When they had put on their bronze armor, they marched on with Poseidon at their head. In his strong hand he gripped his terrible sword, sharp of edge and flashing like lightning. Woe to anyone who meets it in the day of battle; all men shake with fear and keep away from it.

On the other side Hector put the Trojans in array. Then Poseidon and Hector waged fierce war against each other—Hector on the Trojan side and Poseidon on the Argive. The uproar was mighty as the two forces met. The sea came rolling in toward the ships and tents of the Achaeans. But waves do not thunder on the shore more loudly when Boreas drives them with his blast, nor do the flames of a forest fire roar more fiercely when it is well alight on the mountains, nor does the wind bellow with ruder music as it tears through the treetops when it is blowing its hardest, than the terrible shout the Trojans and Achaeans raised as they sprang at one another.

Hector threw his spear first, aiming at Ajax, who was turned full toward him, and he did not miss. The spear struck where two bands crossed Ajax’s chest—the band of his shield and that of his silver-studded sword—and these protected his body. Hector was angry that his spear had been thrown in vain, and he drew back under cover of his men. As he retreated, Ajax son of Telamon struck him with a stone. Many lay about under the men’s feet as they fought, brought there to prop up the sides of the ships as they lay on the shore. Ajax caught up one of them and hit Hector above the rim of his shield, close to the neck. The blow made him spin like a top and reel in every direction. As an oak falls headlong when the lightning flash of father Zeus uproots it, and there is a terrible smell of brimstone—no man standing near can help being dismayed, for a thunderbolt is a very awful thing—so Hector fell to the earth and bit the dust. His spear dropped from his hand, but his shield and helmet stayed fast about his body, and his bronze armor rang around him.

The sons of the Achaeans ran toward him with a loud cry, hoping to drag him away, and they showered darts on the Trojans. But none of them could wound him before he was surrounded and covered by the princes Polydamas, Aeneas, Agenor, Sarpedon captain of the Lycians, and noble Glaucus. None of the others forgot him either, and they held their round shields over him. His comrades lifted him off the ground and carried him from the battle to the place where his horses stood waiting at the rear of the fight with their driver and the chariot. These took him toward the city, groaning in great pain. When they reached the ford of the fair stream of Xanthus, begotten of immortal Zeus, they lifted him from the chariot and laid him on the ground. They poured water over him, and as they did he breathed again and opened his eyes. Then he got up on his knees and vomited blood, but soon fell back on the ground, and his eyes closed again in darkness, for the blow still held him stunned.

When the Argives saw Hector leaving the field, they took heart and attacked the Trojans even more furiously. Swift Ajax son of Oileus led off by springing on Satnius son of Enops and wounding him with his spear. A fair naiad nymph had borne him to Enops while Enops was herding cattle by the banks of the river Satnioeis. The son of Oileus came up and struck him in the flank, so that he fell, and a fierce fight between Trojans and Danaans raged round his body. Polydamas son of Panthous came near to avenge him and wounded Prothoenor son of Areilycus in the right shoulder. The terrible spear went right through the shoulder, and he clutched the earth as he fell in the dust. Polydamas boasted loudly over him: “Once again I think the spear has not flown in vain from the strong hand of the son of Panthous. An Argive has caught it in his body, and it will serve him as a staff on his way down to the house of Hades.”

The Argives were maddened by this boasting. Ajax son of Telamon was angrier than any, because the man had fallen right beside him. He aimed at Polydamas as he retreated, but Polydamas saved himself by swerving aside, and the spear struck Archelochus son of Antenor, for heaven had decided on his destruction. It hit him where the head joins the neck, at the top joint of the spine, and cut through both tendons at the back of the head. His head, mouth and nostrils reached the ground long before his legs and knees could, and Ajax shouted to Polydamas, “Think, Polydamas, and tell me truly: is this man not as well worth killing as Prothoenor was? He seems rich, and of a rich family—a brother, it may be, or a son of the knight Antenor, for he is very like him.”

But he knew well who it was, and the Trojans were greatly angered. Acamas then stood astride his brother’s body and wounded Promachus the Boeotian with his spear, because Promachus was trying to drag the body away. Acamas boasted loudly over him: “Argive archers, braggarts that you are, toil and suffering will not be for us alone. Some of you will fall here as well as we. See how Promachus now sleeps, vanquished by my spear. Payment for my brother’s blood was not long delayed. A man may well be thankful, therefore, if he leaves a kinsman in his house to avenge his fall.”

The Argives were infuriated by his taunts, and Peneleos was more enraged than any of them. He sprang at Acamas, but Acamas did not stand his ground, and Peneleos killed Ilioneus son of the rich flock-master Phorbas, whom Hermes had favored and given more wealth than any other Trojan. Ilioneus was Phorbas’s only son. Peneleos wounded him in the eye under the eyebrows, tearing the eyeball from its socket. The spear went right through the eye into the nape of the neck, and he fell, stretching out both hands in front of him. Peneleos then drew his sword and struck him on the neck, so that head and helmet both tumbled to the ground with the spear still sticking in the eye. He held up the head as though it were a poppy head and showed it to the Trojans, boasting over them as he did. “Trojans,” he cried, “tell the father and mother of noble Ilioneus to mourn for him in their house. The wife of Promachus son of Alegenor will not be gladdened either by her dear husband’s coming, when we Argives sail home from Troy with our ships.”
As he spoke, fear took hold of them all, and each man looked about for a way to escape.

Tell me now, Muses who live on Olympus, who was the first of the Argives to carry off blood-stained spoils after Poseidon, lord of the earthquake, had turned the fortune of war. Ajax son of Telamon was first: he wounded Hyrtius son of Gyrtius, captain of the staunch Mysians. Antilochus killed Phalces and Mermerus, Meriones slew Morys and Hippotion, and Teucer killed Prothoon and Periphetes. The son of Atreus then wounded Hyperenor, shepherd of his people, in the flank. The bronze point tore in among his entrails and made them gush out, and his life came hurrying out of him at the place where he was wounded, and his eyes closed in darkness. Ajax son of Oileus killed more than any other, for no man was so swift as he in chasing down fleeing enemies when Zeus had spread panic among them.
